Honey bees keep the centre of their hive at about 35 degrees Celsius, the warmth that young bees need to grow.
In summer, the temperature outside can rise much higher than this.
When the hive begins to heat up, some workers stand near the entrance and fan their wings.
The moving air pushes warm air out and pulls cooler air in.
Other workers fly to ponds and streams and collect small drops of water.
They spread these drops on the walls of the hive, and as the water dries, it takes heat away.
In winter the problem is the opposite one.
The bees gather in a tight ball around the queen and shiver their flight muscles to make heat.
Bees on the outside of the ball slowly swap places with those in the middle, so that none of them gets too cold.
A colony can survive long cold months in this way as long as it has enough stored honey to fuel the shivering.
